summary: No new sense is needed for human digging, a stone heap or a created pit; the action remains the existing aufkratzen/aufscharren. No foot-kicking sense can be inferred solely from the Syriac etymology.
boʕaṭnoli and bʕəṭlele identify a self-beneficiary without being Detransitive forms. The verb has an overt hole/pit object, contrasting with implicit soil at the cat occurrence.

Three Preterit tokens at 96/258 encode continued scratching, not three independent examples. That verse is incorrectly attached to the existing cat quotation; correction and separate added context preserve both sources.
No II occurrence was supplied; the existing wühlen stem and its b- example remain unchanged. German wühle in the I examples is not grounds for moving their forms to II.

Written biographical/research prose extends concrete digging to investigation. The first context explicitly lacks complete information and seeks something to come to light; the second concerns a report and abstract ties/relations.
b- marks the field/domain at 78; ʕal marks explicit topics at 188. Neither is a new material object or a reason to move the I forms to II.
Round-1 literal digging examples and its cat-citation correction are retained. No new idiom or light-verb noun construction is present.
Check inherited boḥṭət in the wound example against its original grammar source; no matching corpus token here licenses a spelling correction.
Confirm whether objectless scratching and created-hole objects are both ordinary extensions of the same I action; the present corpus supports this grouping.
Is figurative investigation with ʕal-topic broadly productive, or characteristic of this written register? The two Jan passages support the proposed subsense without proving its dialect distribution.

Human subjects open a stone heap or make a pit; these extend the existing scratching/scraping action beyond the cat. Hole/pit objects can denote a created result; self-benefactive suffixes occur in Infectum and Preterit.
